title: How the Internet Actually Moves Your Data
source_text:
Large networks meet physically at internet exchange points, buildings full of routers where they plug into each other and agree to swap traffic. This peering is usually settlement-free between networks of similar size, because both sides gain roughly equal value from the exchange.

Smaller networks that can't peer with everyone instead pay a larger provider for transit: the right to reach the whole internet through that provider's connections. Transit contracts, not any single map, are what actually stitches the mesh together end to end.

Your data is broken into small packets before it leaves your device, each carrying its own address and a piece of the whole message. Routers along the way forward each packet independently, so packets from the same page load can take different paths and still arrive in the right order once reassembled.

Latency is the time a single packet takes to travel from sender to receiver, driven mostly by physical distance and the number of hops in between. Even at the speed of light, a round trip across an ocean adds tens of milliseconds that no amount of bandwidth can remove.

Jitter is the variation in that delay from one packet to the next, usually caused by routers queuing packets differently as network load shifts. A video call can tolerate steady latency far better than it tolerates jitter, because jitter is what actually causes stutter and dropped frames.

When a router's outgoing queue fills up, it starts discarding packets rather than letting the queue grow without bound, a deliberate design choice called active queue management. For real-time video, a dropped packet often matters less than a late one, since a frame that arrives too late is thrown away anyway.

Nobody wants to type a string of numbers to visit a website, so the internet layers a naming system, the Domain Name System or DNS, on top of raw IP addresses. When you type a domain name into a browser, your computer asks a DNS resolver to translate that name into an IP address before any connection can be made. This lookup is usually invisible and fast, cached at several levels, but it is also a common point of failure: if DNS is broken or blocked, a website can be completely unreachable even though the server hosting it is running fine.

DNS is organized as a hierarchy. At the top are root servers that know which servers are authoritative for each top-level domain, such as .com or .org. Those servers in turn know which servers are authoritative for individual domains, and so on down to the specific record for a given subdomain. This structure means no single server needs to store the whole internet's worth of names, and it is part of why the naming system has scaled from a few hundred hosts in the 1980s to billions of names today.

UDP sends packets without any handshake, acknowledgement or guaranteed order, and simply drops anything that doesn't arrive in time. There is no connection to set up and nothing to retransmit, so a UDP packet either arrives quickly or is simply gone.

Live video and voice calls prefer this trade: a late frame is useless anyway, so retransmitting it would only make the stutter worse, not better. Dropping it and moving on keeps the call feeling live instead of feeling behind.

Before any data moves, TCP performs a three-way handshake: the client proposes a starting sequence number, the server acknowledges it and proposes its own, and the client acknowledges that in turn. Only after this handshake do the two sides start exchanging the actual data, each packet numbered so missing or out-of-order packets can be detected and fixed.

TLS runs a second handshake on top of TCP's: the server presents a certificate, the browser checks it against a chain of trust, and the two sides agree on a shared key used to encrypt everything that follows. Without this step, a network in the middle could silently read or alter every request, which is why plain HTTP is considered unsafe for anything sensitive.

Before blaming the network, check whether the domain resolves at all: a failed or wrong DNS answer looks identical to a dead server from the browser's point of view, but the fix is completely different. Tools like dig or nslookup answer this in seconds and rule out an entire category of problems.

A ping confirms whether the destination is reachable at all and roughly how long a round trip takes. It says almost nothing about why a connection is slow, only whether the most basic form of contact succeeds.

A traceroute goes further, showing every router hop along the way, so a connection that dies at the same hop every time usually points at that specific network, not your own. It turns a vague “it doesn't work” into a specific hop to investigate.

Some connections look fine at idle and only drop packets once real traffic load hits a congested link, so a one-off ping is not enough to rule out this kind of failure. Sustained tests, or simply watching a call degrade under load, catch the failures that a single quiet ping misses.

n1.text: The internet is a mesh of independently owned networks that pass packets to each other, not a single wire owned by anyone.
n1.title: Not one pipe, but a mesh
n1.hook: Data doesn't travel one wire; it hops across networks owned by thousands of separate companies.

Independently owned networks interconnect at exchange points

n2.text: Latency, jitter and packet loss compound under load, and video calls suffer first because they can't wait for retransmitted data.
n2.title: Why your video call stutters
n2.hook: Small delays compound because routers queue, drop and reorder packets when a link is busy.

Jitter is delay that varies from packet to packet
Congested routers queue or drop packets under load
